articles.title_orig: Crypto industry braces for reckoning over Trump ties
articles.title_zh: Crypto industry braces for reckoning over Trump ties
articles.content_orig:
This article was contributed by Binance
The second Trump term has put cryptocurrencies on center stage, not only as a policy priority but as a source of real income for the president himself.
The country is suddenly talking about Bitcoin reserves, government-backed stockpiles and Trump’s crypto businesses generating more revenue than his real estate empire. The market is responding in ways not seen before. As of September 25, 2026, the Bitcoin to USD rate was $83,376.06, according to data from Binance. And Washington might have as much influence over the price as basic supply and demand.
In March 2025, Trump signed an executive order creating a Strategic Bitcoin Reserve. This pool was initially filled with Bitcoin already in government hands, seized during various criminal and civil forfeiture cases, according to an official statement from the White House. Alongside that, there’s a Digital Asset Stockpile for other coins. The plan is simple enough: Hold Bitcoin like the U.S. holds gold or oil, and make it a national reserve asset.
More than a year later, this reserve is still mostly for show. The administration keeps insisting that Congress needs to step in before things take off, and while a bill is expected to be reintroduced under a fresh name, so far it’s all been talk, according to Yahoo Finance. Early numbers suggested the government had about 200,000 BTC, though the U.S. Marshals Service isn’t so sure about that, according to CCN.
That Bitcoin reserve was just the warm-up. In July 2025, Trump greenlit the GENIUS Act, the first real federal framework for stablecoins backed by U.S. dollars. Now, payment stablecoins get official recognition: They’re neither securities nor commodities, finally cutting through years of confusion, according to a fact sheet from the White House.
Banks, asset managers and large corporations have shown renewed interest in stablecoins following the regulatory clarity. Regulated stablecoins are becoming a preferred tool for settling tokenized securities and on-chain payments, a shift that could open the door to significant new capital, according to Yahoo Finance and Investing.com. The Trump administration has also appointed crypto-friendly regulators across federal agencies. In May 2026, Trump signed another executive order requiring regulators to drop rules that kept banks from partnering with fintech and crypto companies, according to a fact sheet from the White House .
All these regulatory resets have supercharged the industry and Trump’s business interests. His 2025 financial disclosure, sent to the Office of Government Ethics and made public on June 30, 2026, shows digital assets as his top income stream. His companies pulled in nearly $800 million from World Liberty Financial, the crypto project he co-founded with his sons. That includes $520 million from token sales, and another $250 million by selling stakes in the venture. On top of that, Trump scored another $635 million through sales of the $TRUMP meme coin, which he launched just before returning to office. All this has been reported by Time and Reuters.
Sum it up, and Trump’s family crypto businesses brought in more than $1.4 billion in reported income for 2025. Reuters says crypto was the single biggest driver of his $2.2 billion in total disclosed earnings, beating out real estate and legal settlements combined. When he was called out for it, Trump told reporters, “You know why I’m profiting, because the stock market’s going up, everybody’s profiting,” according to Reuters. For context, his crypto income from the same venture in 2024 was about $57 million, so it grew more than tenfold in just one year, riding the wave of policy changes, according to BBC.
It’s not just empty promises. Companies in the sector have started making real moves thanks to regulatory clarity. Stablecoin issuers, payment platforms and crypto on/off ramp providers are citing the GENIUS Act as the reason they’re ramping up U.S. operations instead of dodging them, according to The Economic Times.
Banks that used to steer clear of crypto because of a 2022 FDIC directive can now roll out digital asset products that follow the rules, according to Legal500.
Dollar moves matter to Bitcoin buyers. The Press Banner’s money column on protecting your portfolio from a falling dollar covers the same concern that has drawn some investors toward Bitcoin during Trump’s second term.
Has the U.S. government bought more Bitcoin for its reserve?
No, not yet. The Strategic Bitcoin Reserve, created in March 2025, only includes Bitcoin seized through criminal and civil cases.
Does the GENIUS Act regulate Bitcoin itself?
No. The GENIUS Act is purely about U.S. dollar-backed stablecoins. It forces issuers to back their tokens one-to-one with cash and Treasury securities, and to publish monthly reserve reports.
How much has Bitcoin moved in September 2026 alone?
It ran from about $76,800 on September 2 to $83,376.06 on September 25, 2026, according to Binance.

articles.title_orig: Ukraine war briefing: Russia ramping up attacks to ‘pressure’ Kyiv at trilateral talks, Zelenskyy says
articles.title_zh: Ukraine war briefing: Russia ramping up attacks to ‘pressure’ Kyiv at trilateral talks, Zelenskyy says
articles.content_orig:
President urges US for support, saying ‘Ukraine must not be left to face this alone’ as barrage plunges cities into darkness. What we know on day 1,719
Volodymyr Zelenskyy has accused Russia of intensifying strikes across the country to put pressure on Kyiv at upcoming talks after an overnight barrage triggered power cuts as temperatures drop. “By intensifying its attacks on Ukraine and our infrastructure at this very moment, Russia is trying to additionally lay the groundwork for putting pressure on Ukraine’s position and that of its partners,” the Ukrainian president said. “Russia perceives diplomacy in its own peculiar way – as a form of aggression.”
Ukraine’s energy ministry said “a massive attack on a number of energy facilities” on Saturday had plunged five regions into darkness and significantly hampered electricity transmission in Kyiv and surrounding regions. Russia had throughout the night launched 172 drones and 36 ballistic missiles, Zelenskyy said, among which were KN-23 missiles manufactured and supplied by North Korea.
The strikes came before a US-brokered trilateral meeting in Abu Dhabi scheduled for next week aimed at reviving stalled diplomatic efforts towards peace. Ukrainian officials are expected to sit down with Russian negotiators and US envoys on Tuesday and Wednesday for the first such talks in months. The diplomatic track has been stalled since February when Washington shifted attention to its war with Iran.
Zelenskyy also urged the US to increase its flagging aid to Ukraine. “Unfortunately, there is still a significant shortage of interceptors for Patriot systems, and the United States is in the best position to help address it,” he said.
Italy’s foreign minister, Antonio Tajani , on Saturday said he had been targeted by pro-Russian hackers over his backing for Ukraine . Tajani said in a post on X that “backing in a transparent way the freedom and independence of a sovereign state” had made him a target. Tajani said his personal data had been published on the dark web and that the hackers were seeking further information about him and his family and were ‌willing to pay for it.
The Italian prime minister, Giorgia Meloni, who has been one of the strongest backers of Ukraine among western leaders, expressed her support for Tajani and said the sale of confidential information relating to public officials was “a matter of serious concern”. Moscow has not commented ‌on the incident. ‌
France’s far-left presidential contender Jean-Luc Mélenchon said on Saturday that settling the Ukraine conflict could not be done by granting territorial concessions without consulting the people concerned . Melenchon, who polls suggest could reach the second round of next year’s presidential election, set out his France Unbowed party’s foreign policy positions at a rally just outside Paris.
Mélenchon has been criticised in the past for questioning the legitimacy of Zelenskyy. But in a campaign speech to thousands of supporters, he said an administration run by his party would take an active role in settling the war in Ukraine . Europe would have to play an active role in peace talks, he said. “We cannot accept that one could consider a peace with territorial concessions in Ukraine without asking the populations concerned if they agree or not to be on one side or other of the border,” he said. “It is for the people themselves to decide what they want,” he added.
A Ukrainian attack killed one person in Russia’s Belgorod region when a drone hit a private home in the town of Grayvoron, local officials said on Saturday. Russia’s defence ministry said its forces shot down 411 Ukrainian drones overnight over 10 Russian regions, including Belgorod. Drones were also destroyed over the annexed Ukrainian peninsula of Crimea and the Black and Azov seas, it said. Russian media outlets later reported that the Saratov Oil Refinery had been hit and shared images of plumes of smoke over the city.

articles.title_orig: Ten Months of War to Gain 46 Square Miles: How Russia Is Failing on the Battlefield
articles.title_zh: Ten Months of War to Gain 46 Square Miles: How Russia Is Failing on the Battlefield
articles.content_orig:
Russian Offensive Campaign Assessment
Russian forces continued their missile and drone strike campaign against Ukraine’s energy infrastructure and targeted Kyiv City with 36 ballistic missiles overnight on November 6 to 7. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky stated that Russian forces conducted a massive missile and drone strike campaign against Ukraine overnight, primarily targeting Kyiv City and Ukraine’s energy infrastructure.[1] Zelensky specified that Russian forces targeted 13 oblasts in total, launched 172 drones and 36 ballistic missiles, and that all missiles targeted Kyiv City and Kyiv Oblast. Zelensky stated that Russian strikes damaged an electricity substation in Kyiv Oblast connecting the Rivne and Khmelnytskyi nuclear power plants with Kyiv City and Ukraine’s central oblasts and struck substations in Vinnytsia, Zhytomyr, Rivne, Kharkiv, and Dnipropetrovsk oblasts. The Russian Ministry of Defense (MoD) claimed on November 7 that Russian forces struck the Trypilska Thermal Power Plant and the Kyivska and Northern electrical substations in Kyiv Oblast as well as an electrical substation in Zhytomyr Oblast.[2] Russia‘s deliberate targeting of Ukraine’s energy infrastructure corroborates an unconfirmed, intercepted Russian plan that Russian forces would systematically attempt to strike Ukrainian electricity generation and transmission facilities to disconnect Ukraine’s nuclear power plants from a unified grid and cut off Kyiv City from external power supplies.[3] Russia has been increasingly incorporating turbojet engines and mesh radio modems into its long-range strike drones, which is likely allowing Russian forces to more effectively penetrate Ukrainian air defenses and conduct more precise strikes compared to Russia’s Winter 2025-2026 strike campaign. The depletion of Ukraine’s missile interceptors and limited counter-launch capabilities risk leaving Ukraine vulnerable to Russian ballistic missile strikes.
The large-scale Russian ballistic missile strike against Kyiv City also damaged the Northern Bridge, as Russian forces continue efforts to target Ukraine’s transportation infrastructure and disrupt its economy. Kyiv City Mayor Vitaliy Klitschko reported on November 7 that Russian forces damaged the roadbed, trolleybus overhead line, and power line at the Northern Bridge across the Dnipro River in the city.[4] Zelensky stated that Russian forces launched six ballistic missiles at the bridge, four of which struck it.[5] Geolocated footage published on November 7 shows extensive damage to the bridge.[6] Russian forces have repeatedly struck Kyiv City’s Northern and Southern bridges throughout October 2026.[7] Such strikes aim to disrupt the wider Ukrainian economy, sow panic among the population, and significantly degrade civilian life and movement in Ukraine‘s capital.
Ukrainian forces are targeting missile launch sites and ballistic missile production facilities in Russia to reduce Russia’s ability to conduct devastating ballistic missile strikes amidst Ukraine’s dwindling air defense stockpiles. Ukrainian forces struck two Iskander missile launchers and a Pantsir-S1 air defense system in Bryansk Oblast on November 6 and overnight from November 6 to 7, according to the Ukrainian General Staff.[8] The General Staff also reported that Ukrainian forces launched a Neptune cruise missile strike against the Proton-Electrotex Plant in Oryol City, Oryol Oblast (roughly 160 kilometers from the international border), overnight.[9] The Proton-Electrotex Plant produces optoelectronic equipment, including parts for Iskander-M ballistic missiles. Ukraine’s ability to conduct long-range strikes against military assets in Russia is critical for Ukrainian defense against Russian missile strikes ahead of the likely difficult Winter 2026-2027, particularly as Russia’s missile production rate remains high. Ukraine’s Main Military Intelligence Directorate (GUR) reported that Russian forces have stockpiled up to 700 ballistic missiles as of October 2026 and that Russia’s Iskander-M ballistic missile stockpile increased by 13 percent in October compared to August 2026.[10] The GUR added that Russia produces 65 Iskander-M missiles per month.
Western support, including the provision of air defense systems and interceptors, long-range missiles, and reliable low-latency satellite access over Russia, remains vital to Ukraine’s ability to significantly degrade Russia’s drone and missile strike capabilities. The provision of US Tomahawk missiles, for example, would allow Ukraine to strike important military infrastructure that Russia protects in its rear, as ISW has long assessed.[11] Zelensky similarly called on November 5 for Germany to provide Ukraine with Taurus cruise missiles to support the Ukrainian strike campaign against Russian ballistic missile launchers.[12] Even a relatively small number of Western-provided missiles could allow Ukraine to begin systematically targeting Russia’s drone production facilities at the Alabuga Special Economic Zone (SEZ) in the Republic of Tatarstan or the Engels-2 Air Base in Saratov Oblast that houses strategic bombers, which Russian forces use to launch cruise missiles against Ukraine. Ukraine has been using its long-range drones and domestically produced cruise missiles to strike targets deep in the Russian rear, and further Western support would allow Ukraine to degrade Russia’s long-range strike capabilities.
Ukrainian and Russian officials provided further details about the composition of the delegations for the upcoming trilateral negotiations scheduled for November 10 to 11 in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates (UAE). Ukrainian Servant of the People Party Head Davyd Arakhamia stated on November 6 that Foreign Intelligence Service Head Rustem Umerov will lead the Ukrainian delegation, which will also include Presidential Communications Adviser Dmytro Lytvyn, Presidential Office Head Kyrylo Budanov, and Presidential Office First Deputy Head Serhiy Kyslytsya.[13] Russian President Vladimir Putin met with the Russian delegation on November 6, which will include Presidential Aide Vladimir Medinsky, General Staff’s Main Directorate (GRU) Head Admiral Igor Kostyukov, Presidential Aide Yuriy Ushakov, and Deputy Foreign Ministers Mikhail Galuzin and Sergei Ryabkov.[14] Kostyukov led the Russian delegation at the first two rounds of trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi in late January and early February 2026 before Medinsky replaced him to lead the Russian delegation at trilateral negotiations in Geneva, Switzerland, in February 2026. Medinsky notably used his position to stall negotiations by discussing the so-called “historical roots” of the war, the Kremlin’s shorthand for its original maximalist demands.[15] Ushakov is a senior Kremlin official who regularly comments on the status of negotiations with Ukraine and has repeatedly reiterated the Kremlin’s maximalist demands that Ukraine make unilateral concessions before Russia agrees to engage in any meaningful peace negotiations.[16] Galuzin was a member of the Russian delegation to negotiations in Istanbul, Turkey, as well as Geneva in May 2025 and February 2026, respectively, and has reiterated the need to address the so-called “root causes” of the war.[17] Ryabkov has not formally participated in peace negotiations but frequently claims that Russia can only accept peace proposals that align with Putin’s war aims and “ground realities.” Ryabkov routinely reiterates Russia’s commitment to the alleged US-Russia agreements following the Alaska Summit in August 2025, despite the lack of public statements following the summit and no confirmation that any agreement was reached.[18] Ryabkov also facilitated the Kremlin’s 2021 ultimatums to the United States and NATO member states, which amounted to the destruction of the current NATO alliance under the guise of “security guarantees” for Russia.[19] The Kremlin appears to be sending a delegation of officials who previously stalled neg

articles.title_orig: President Herzog taps Eisenkot to form coalition, but path remains fraught
articles.title_zh: President Herzog taps Eisenkot to form coalition, but path remains fraught
articles.content_orig:
In a setback to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu , his main rival will be tasked with forming the next Israeli government, placing him one step closer to ousting Israel’s longest-serving leader, even as the path remains complicated.
Gadi Eisenkot , a retired military chief who led the centrist Yashar party in the October 27 election, will have up to six weeks to try and assemble a coalition to replace Netanyahu. But his path to power is fraught with political obstacles and divisions within the opposition itself.
President Isaac Herzog will officially give Eisenkot the mandate to form a government on Sunday, his office said in a statement. Herzog’s decision followed two days of consultations last week with all parties elected to the Knesset.
Eisenkot secured the support of 67 members of the incoming Knesset, including 19 from the two Arab parties. Netanyahu received just 46 recommendations. A notable crack in his once-loyal bloc was exposed during the consultations when United Torah Judaism, a traditional Netanyahu ally, declined to recommend him.
Yet Herzog’s decision does not automatically remove Netanyahu from power. Eisenkot has a mandate and a parliamentary majority on paper, but not yet a governing coalition.
Eisenkot is pushing to form what he calls a “national emergency government” and to swear in a minority government as soon as possible. It would comprise the four Jewish opposition parties, which together hold 48 seats: his own Yashar; Together, led by former prime ministers Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid; Avigdor Liberman’s Yisrael Beiteinu, and the left-wing Democrats, led by Yair Golan.
He has set four conditions for joining: recognizing Israel as a Jewish, democratic, liberal, and egalitarian state, commitment to the values of the Declaration of Independence, universal service – whether military, national, or civilian – and recognition of Hamas as a terrorist organization.
The last condition effectively rules out the Arab parties from sitting in the Cabinet. But they could still support the government from outside, providing a parliamentary safety net. Israeli law requires only a simple majority to establish a government. Removing one is far more difficult, requires an absolute majority of 61 votes who support an alternative government. (The Knesset has 120 seats.)
Eisenkot’s central obstacle is Avigdor Liberman. The Yisrael Beitenu leader and, at different times, former defense, foreign affairs and finance minister, has ruled out any government dependent on the Arab parties. A minority government, he argues, will be short-lived, and in the long run, will only strengthen Netanyahu. “We’ll have Netanyahu come back with 70 seats for another four years, and from there it’s a short road to annihilation,” Liberman wrote on X on Friday.
Instead, Liberman proposed a different route. Dropping his years-long veto on the ultra-Orthodox parties, he urged to make a “maximum effort” to form a coalition of 61 lawmakers with the two ultra-Orthodox parties, Shas and United Torah Judaism, and without the Joint List and Ra’am. Once it is formed, he added, three or four lawmakers from the Likud may defect.
Trump’s Election Day bombshell on Israel points to historic shift in US politics
That plan, however, clashes with one of the opposition’s core commitments: to end the blanket draft exemption for ultra-Orthodox men from mandatory military service. The ultra-Orthodox parties are pressing for legislation that would enshrine the exemption, and Eisenkot, Liberman and the rest of the opposition pledged universal service throughout the campaign. Moreover, one of the ultra-Orthodox parties remains loyal to Netanyahu.
Netanyahu, who lost his parliamentary majority, is also applying heavy pressure against any Jewish-Arab political cooperation. He is challenging the election results and claims the vote was “stolen” by Arab parties by bribery and foreign funding. David Zini, his loyalist Shin Bet director, has been pushing to investigate Arab politicians without any public evidence.
In a video statement Saturday, Netanyahu warned that if a minority government is formed with the Arab parties’ support, Israel will “simply not survive.” Instead, he called for a national unity government with his entire bloc, which includes far-right and ultra-Orthodox parties. Netanyahu called for “all Zionist parties that want to preserve our one and only state of the Jewish people.”
Eisenkot dismissed his message as a “pathetic spin.” In a statement, the Yashar party said, “If the Likud wants a broad unity government, it is more than welcome to announce the dissolution of the alliance with the extremists and enter a government under Prime Minister Eisenkot.”
Eisenkot’s first test comes Tuesday with the swearing in of the new Knesset. The opposition intends to replace Netanyahu’s Knesset speaker, weakening his grip on power and allowing the opposition parties to begin taking some actions, such as forming a state commission of inquiry into the security failures that led to the October 7, 2023, attack by Hamas. Starting Sunday, Eisenkot will have 28 days to negotiate with other parties over Cabinet posts, budgets and policies, with a possible 14-day extension. If he fails, the mandate passes to Netanyahu for another four weeks.
Eisenkot said on Friday he intends to form a government as quickly as possible, framing the moment as a national emergency. “A situation in which a caretaker prime minister in the minority, who has lost the trust of the people in such an extreme way, continues to operate the security system and law enforcement authorities, is a dangerous situation that must not continue even for one more day,” he wrote on X.

articles.title_orig: Drone and missile attacks wound 9 in Ukraine as country prepares for talks with Russia and US
articles.title_zh: Drone and missile attacks wound 9 in Ukraine as country prepares for talks with Russia and US
articles.content_orig:
Moscow used 172 drones and 36 ballistic missiles in attacks on electricity substations and bridge over the Dnipro
Volodymyr Zelenskyy has accused Russia of trying to “plunge Kyiv and the entire country into a blackout”, after a major attack overnight on energy infrastructure in the capital and a bridge over the Dnipro River.
Ukraine’s president said Moscow’s preparations for peace talks next week involved pummelling a city of millions with ballistic missiles.
Negotiators from Russia , Ukraine and the US are due to meet on Tuesday and Wednesday in Abu Dhabi, the capital of the United Arab Emirates, for talks aimed at ending the war.
Zelenskyy appealed to the US Congress – won by the Democrats in the midterm elections – to pay more attention to Ukraine in the face of relentless Russian bombardment. “Ukraine must not be left alone. We are counting on increased bilateral support from the US,” he said .
Russia used 172 drones and 36 ballistic missiles in its latest attack on Kyiv and surrounding regions. The city faced serious difficulties with its electricity, water and heat supplies, Zelenskyy said, with five people injured including a 14-year-old girl.
The strikes targeted substations in five regions, including one connecting two nuclear power plants to Kyiv. The city’s Northern Bridge, a key transport artery, was closed on Saturday as workers repaired damage to the road’s surface and power lines.
The attacks cap a dire week for residents in Kyiv, who have experienced day-long power cuts and interruptions to the water supply. Ukrainian officials say the Kremlin’s goal is to freeze civilians into submission over the brutal winter months, a war crime.
They have little confidence that US-backed peace talks will yield concrete results. In an interview with CNN , Zelenskyy described the latest blueprint set out by Jared Kushner, Donald Trump’s son-in-law, as “Yalta 2.0” – a reference to the 1945 summit between Stalin, Roosevelt and Churchill that divided postwar Europe.
In a series of social media posts , Kushner said the discussions would include a new security framework for Europe, alongside guarantees for Ukraine. This appears to be a reference to the Kremlin’s longstanding demand that Nato’s expansion across Europe be reversed.
after newsletter promotion
Speaking on Friday, Trump said a “big beautiful agreement” could be close, involving “all of Europe”. Shortly before invading Ukraine, the Russian president, Vladimir Putin, demanded that Nato go back to its pre-1997 posture – before the Baltic states and nations in eastern Europe and the Balkans joined.
Ukraine and its European partners are deeply sceptical. “The idea of discussing European-Russian security infrastructure is not simple, and it can be dangerous,” Zelenskyy told CNN, emphasising: “We don’t want to be divided by Russia.”
Zelenskyy said Moscow had to end its war first, with Ukraine given meaningful security guarantees. After that, “depending on the answers”, wider security architecture could be considered, he said. Western diplomats say agreeing to Russia’s demands would effectively end Nato.
Russia’s defence ministry, meanwhile, said its strikes early on Saturday were against energy and transport targets. Since the summer, it has dramatically stepped up air attacks on Ukrainian cities, as its progress on the frontline has stalled. Last month Russia lost 54,000 troops, killed or injured, according to Kyiv – the highest monthly loss in the war.

Rock shows, Del Boy and his three-wheeler from Only Fools and Horses, and a circus big top were among the themes showcased during a spectacular illuminated carnival procession.
Thousands of people watched the event in Bridgwater, Somerset, where clubs spend the entire year preparing carts for the show.
Dan Prosser from the Renegades Carnival Club said the preparations were "more like a lifestyle than just a hobby," adding his non-carnival friends think his devotion to the event is "absolutely nuts".
The carnival ended with 210 people - including local MP Sir Ashley Fox - taking part in squibbing, where a large firework, strapped to a solid block of wood on the end of a pole, is lit.

articles.title_orig: King Charles would ‘carefully’ consider China visit
articles.title_zh: King Charles would ‘carefully’ consider China visit
articles.content_orig:
By REBECCA ENGLISH, ROYAL EDITOR and GLEN OWEN
Published: 18:29 EDT, 7 November 2026 | Updated: 18:59 EDT, 7 November 2026
King Charles would be prepared to undertake a controversial state visit to China if requested by Prime Minister Andy Burnham , sources indicated on Saturday.
As Charles is recovering from his 'challenging' Caribbean tour dominated by rows over slavery reparations, Buckingham Palace was not ruling out an even more politically testing trip to Beijing .
Such a visit would be the first by a British monarch to the communist country for 40 years, but would be fraught with controversy given the ongoing security threat posed by China to Britain. One Whitehall source told The Mail on Sunday: 'We understand the King would be quite up for it, if it came to it.'
But a senior Tory source said: 'This would be seen as seriously divisive politics.'
Royal insiders stress a trip isn't on the table yet and would come with 'complex' logistical and political issues to navigate.
As Prince of Wales, Charles made no secret of his antipathy to the Chinese regime. But a royal aide said: 'If the government said 'Will the King go to China?' I think we would think about it very carefully.
'China is a hugely important country... a very complex country. It would pose a lot of complexity in putting a programme together. This is the 40th anniversary of the last state visit.'
It comes amid a battle within the Government over whether to confront or appease Beijing. Security officials have complained that Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband is leading the 'appease' camp as the UK is so reliant on China for the supply of solar panels central to his Net Zero climate agenda.
King Charles III during his tour of Antigua and Barbuda. The Palace has not ruled the King travelling on a politically testing trip to Beijing
Prime Minister Andy Burnham. A battle is raging within the Government over whether to confront or appease Beijing
As heir to the throne, Charles maintained a highly–critical stance over the Chinese government, particularly as a result of his support for Tibet and the Dalai Lama. He boycotted UK state banquets for presidents Jiang Zemin in 1999 and Hu Jintao in 2005 over China's human rights record.
He once described Chinese officials as 'appalling old waxworks', and also wriggled out of a state banquet to honour president Xi Jinping in 2015.
Despite mounting evidence of state–sponsored activities in the UK, such as cyber attacks and political infiltration, Mr Miliband supports closer ties with China. One of his first moves as Foreign Secretary was to arrange to meet Chinese foreign minister Wang Yi.
Former Tory leader Iain Duncan Smith said: 'If it is true the King might be going to China it is utterly appalling. They are effectively at war with us, and should not be rewarded for it.'
Diplomats believe the King's Caribbean tour was a success, particularly his visit to Guyana, where he was welcomed with open arms at a time when China is making huge inroads in the region.
If rumours are correct, the King is to be wheeled out as Britain's version of 'panda diplomacy' and sent to Communist China.
Is this a state visit too far? I think it is. The issue is not Charles. He has shown himself a master of sensitive visits, whether to the US under erratic Donald Trump or to the Caribbean, where slavery reparations dominated discussion.
No, the question is: why are we debasing ourselves by offering a visit to a China leadership that behaves so destructively towards us? It would be ironic. The debate about historic slavery in the Caribbean pales against China's record of using forced labour now in its cotton and potentially other industries, including silicon used in solar panels that Net Zero fanatic Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband wants to cover the British countryside with. And we reward this with a state visit?
Too often our leaders, especially on the Left, continue the delusion that China is an economic El Dorado which will make us rich. But Beijing does not want free trade. It wants to make others dependent on it. This is not trade as a tool of joint prosperity but trade as a weapon in conflict.
Rather than organising a cringeworthy visit, our leaders' time would be better spent standing up for our values and interests and articulating them clearly.

articles.title_orig: Iran says it has lifted its self-imposed limit on missile ranges, and other Mideast news
articles.title_zh: Iran says it has lifted its self-imposed limit on missile ranges, and other Mideast news
articles.content_orig:
Iran's Revolutionary Guards said Saturday that restrictions on the range of the country's ballistic missiles had been lifted, raising the prospect of strikes against targets farther afield if US or Israeli attacks resume.
Iran has long maintained that it voluntarily restricted the range of its ballistic missiles to 2,000 kilometres (about 1,200 miles), sufficient to reach Israel and US military installations across much of the Middle East.
Referring to a recent directive from Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei to respond to threats with “no geographical limits,” IRGC spokesman Hossein Mohebbi said: “That restriction has been lifted for us.”
He did not say whether Iran had developed or deployed missiles capable of exceeding its previously declared range limit, saying only that the country's capabilities should be demonstrated in practice, not through public statements.
Ali Bilali, an adviser to the commander of the IRGC Aerospace Force, said Saturday that Iran's missiles had a range of about 2,000 kilometres and were capable of precision strikes.
The question of whether Iran possesses longer-range weapons gained prominence during the war in March, when US and British officials said two ballistic missiles had been launched towards Diego Garcia, a joint American-British military base in the Indian Ocean nearly 4,000 kilometres from Iranian territory.
British Defence Secretary John Healey said one fell short and the other was intercepted before reaching its target. Iran denied responsibility for the attempted strike.
Iran's ballistic missile programme has repeatedly featured in US demands for restrictions on Tehran's military capabilities, although it appears to have receded from more recent diplomatic proposals, which have focused primarily on the nuclear programme.
Missiles are central to Iran's military deterrence, especially after two rounds of war that severely degraded its air defences and other conventional capabilities.
Regional powers, including Saudi Arabia, Qatar and Turkey, press for a negotiated settlement between Tehran and Washington, seeking to avert another round of fighting that could threaten their security, disrupt energy supplies and inflict further economic damage across the region.
Speaking at a news conference marking the IRGC's Aerospace Week, Mohebbi said the late Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei had previously directed the military to halt increases in missile range at certain times and authorised extensions at others.
He also claimed that the Guards had moved missile and drone production underground during the wars with Israel and the United States, allowing manufacturing to continue despite bombardment.
“Any point from which we sense a serious threat against our country can become our target,” Mohebbi said, warning that further attacks on Iran would carry a heavy price for its adversaries.
The report, which the channel said was unsourced and broadcast under military censorship, did not describe the operation. It said other senior figures in the security establishment opposed it because it could cause an escalation and force the election to be postponed, but that planning went ahead until the United States learned of it and moved to stop it.
The Prime Minister's Office denied the report: "The prime minister himself clarified in real time that an attack before the Israeli elections was not on the agenda."
The account follows a run of reports in the week of the vote. On October 25, two days before the election, Channel 12 reported an "unprecedented confrontation" between Benjamin Netanyahuand the military chief of staff, Eyal Zamir, over an instruction for unspecified action involving Iran, with Zamir demanding further deliberations and signed legal authorization.
Iran International carried that report at the time. The next day Channels 12 and 13 reported that Zamir was the only security chief to oppose the action, and the New York Times reported, citing three senior defense officials, that Netanyahu had "sought for weeks to orchestrate a new airstrike on Iran" and was blocked by Zamir.
CNN reported that Netanyahu had asked President Donald Trump to approve a joint strike before the election and that Trump refused.
Netanyahu called the October 25 report "nonsense," saying in the same interview that he had "instructed the IDF and Mossad to topple the regime" in Iran. Former prime minister Ehud Barak said on Thursday that Netanyahu had planned "a provocation" via the Mossad "behind the back of the IDF chief of staff."
Friday's report came as Qatari-mediated talks between Washington and Tehran continued. Channel 12 reported this week that Netanyahu had urged Trump to resume the war immediately after Tuesday's US midterm elections, and that Trump wanted to give the talks more time.
"We're talking to Iran," Trump told reporters on Friday. "We haven't lost a soldier in six or seven months."
In a post on X on Wednesday, Vance identified ending the war and reassessing relations with Israel among the priorities of voters who supported Donald Trump in 2024 but switched to Democrats in Tuesday's midterm elections.
Iran's parliament speaker and chief negotiator, Mohammad-Bagher Ghalibaf, quoted Vance's post to challenge the Trump administration's approach to the war and its relationship with Israel.
Iranian media have since offered differing interpretations of Vance's intentions and his influence over US policy.
The analytical website Vana News said the vice president's remarks highlighted differences in how senior US officials assessed the costs and future of the war, but cautioned against interpreting them as evidence of an irreconcilable rift.
“Differences in perspective do not necessarily mean a breakdown in political cooperation or an irreconcilable conflict between the president and his deputy,” Vana News wrote, adding that it remained unclear whether such differences would affect Washington's policy decisions.
Mohsen Zahedi-Movahed, a retired diplomat and international affairs analyst, was more emphatic.
“Vance's admission that the war was the first reason voters were angry with Republicans is extremely important. How will Trump respond? The divide they wanted to create among Iranian leaders has now come back to haunt them!” he wrote on X.
Ali Nasri, a pro-government commentator, argued that Vance's apparent differences with Trump over Israel predated the Republican election defeat.
“[Vance realised] that his own political future and the survival of the entire America First movement depend on distancing himself from Israel and ending the war with Iran,” Nasri wrote on X. “We paid a heavy price to reach this position of strength,” he added.
But Parisa Nasr, a hardline journalist, warned against interpreting Vance's remarks as an encouraging sign, describing them as “another episode in Vance's double game.”
She accused Vance of pursuing an electoral and geopolitical manoeuvre designed to appeal to American voters while encouraging Iranian officials who favour an agreement with Washington.
Nasr also linked the remarks to mediation efforts by Qatar and Pakistan, warning that Tehran could be drawn into an agreement that would leave it vulnerable to renewed conflict.
“Even if it leads to an immediate asymmetric agreement, it is a prelude to the next war and poses a very serious danger,” she wrote.
Asked on Wednesday whether he agreed that the war had contributed to the Republicans' defeat, Trump said it was “largely true” but defended his decision to attack Iran, insisting that military action was necessary to prevent Tehran from acquiring a nuclear weapon.
The debate over Vance's intentions comes against the backdrop of a letter he sent in late October to Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, to which Tehran has not formally responded.

Pope Leo began an emotionally charged tour of South America on Friday, returning to a continent that helped shape his priesthood just three weeks after undergoing lung cancer surgery.
The 71-year-old head of the Catholic Church will visit Uruguay, Argentina and Peru over 12 days in one of the most intense papal foreign trips in decades, meeting political leaders, prisoners, the poor, as well as old friends.
“I’m very happy to be here,” Leo told reporters on the plane before landing in Uruguay, saying he wanted to bring a “message of hope in today’s world”.

articles.title_orig: Paris agitators defy police orders, renew nationwide protests centered in Paris
articles.title_zh: Paris agitators defy police orders, renew nationwide protests centered in Paris
articles.content_orig:
France’s protest movement is showing little sign of easing, nearly two months after high school students first walked out over crumbling classrooms.
On Saturday , 146,000 people rallied across the country, including 46,000 in Paris, according to the Ministry of the Interior, while unions put the figures at 250,000 and 75,000.
Turnout was down from previous weeks, but police used tear gas and batons on protesters in Paris and fired tear gas canisters at hundreds of people blocking a road in central Lyon, France’s third-largest city. About 70,000 security personnel were deployed, days after an estimated 575,000 people joined a union-organised rally.
The protests have expanded to cover a range of issues, from high fuel prices to wages and social housing, and in some cases, the demonstrations have been marred by looting and violence. Police have been accused of using excessive force, with officers using barricades, tear gas and batons against protesters.
Al Jazeera maps where demonstrations, including riots, have taken place across Europe.
An analysis of data from Armed Conflict Location & Event Data (ACLED) found that between September 15 and October 30, more than 1,200 protests and riots of 100 or more people took place across France over education, public services and the cost of living.
The movement began in mid-September in high schools, where students complained of overcrowded classrooms, a lack of teachers and crumbling buildings. It soon broadened into protests against the rising cost of living, drawing in trade unions and the “yellow vests” movement, with rioting and looting on the sidelines.
On October 17 alone, more than 500,000 people protested nationwide, according to government estimates.
ACLED CEO Clionadh Raleigh said on October 19 that ACLED had recorded an average of 20.5 demonstrations a day in France over the past five years. “During the current protest cycle, that has jumped to almost 66 a day, more than three times the usual rate,” she said.
Protest cycles typically last about 20 days, or 36 for major movements, Raleigh said. By ACLED’s count, this one had reached 45 days and was still going.
“But the most striking difference is the level of confrontation,” she said. “Almost a quarter of events, 24.2 percent, have been classified as riots, compared to a median of just 1.9 percent in previous cycles. Only the unrest following the death of Nahel Merzouk in 2023 recorded a higher proportion.”
The police response has also drawn criticism. On October 28, four United Nations experts mandated by the Human Rights Council expressed alarm at the “excessive use of force” by French authorities in dispersing the student protests.
“The scale of the arrests and detention, affecting several thousand people, mainly minors, appears disproportionate and deters demonstrators from exercising their freedoms of expression and peaceful assembly,” they said in a statement .
In the northern city of Lille, a teenager lost a hand when a grenade exploded as school protesters clashed with police.
France is not protesting alone. Since mid-September, demonstrations over rising living costs, low wages and a lack of public services have broken out in 30 other European countries, from Portugal to Poland.
Between September 15 and October 30, more than 1,700 protests and riots of 100 or more people took place across Europe, according to an analysis of ACLED data.
Although protests in other countries did not reach the same scale as the rallies in France, they may be a sign of discontent spilling over, Alberto Alemanno, professor of European Union law and policy at HEC Paris Business School, told Al Jazeera last month.
“France is the epicentre of this movement … and there are signs now that this is spreading beyond France,” Alemanno said.
France has led the demonstrations, but protests have also broken out across Europe at the same time, driven by a common thread of underfunded education, rising living costs and unaffordable housing.
According to an analysis of ACLED data, France saw more than 1,200 protests and riots between September 15 and October 30, followed by Spain (173), Italy (160), Germany (70) and Portugal (33).
In Spain, tens of thousands of people rallied in early October after parliament rejected two emergency housing decrees on October 2, dealing a blow to Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez’s minority government.
In Italy, demonstrations over the cost-of-living crisis and unaffordable housing have led to clashes with police.
In Portugal, tens of thousands of protesters marched against the cost-of-living crisis, low wages and an inability to access housing in major cities.

articles.title_orig: Paraguay's President Santiago Peña impeached and under house arrest
articles.title_zh: Paraguay's President Santiago Peña impeached and under house arrest
articles.content_orig:
Prosecutors in Paraguay have charged former president Santiago Peña over his alleged role in a banking scandal that led to his impeachment.
He has been accused of breach of trust and administration for personal gain.
Peña, who denies any wrongdoing, was forced from office after a bank collapse triggered a crisis that left more than half of the country's population without access to their accounts.
He was arrested on Friday minutes after lawmakers, including from his own party, unanimously voted to remove him from office following the collapse of Ueno Bank, which has links to his private business interests.
He had offered to step down but rather than accept his resignation, senators impeached Peña and charged him with misconduct, meaning he has been stripped of the immunity usually granted to ex-presidents.
Peña, who until last year held shares in the company that owned the bank, has denied any wrongdoing.
The impeachment charges that led to Peña's removal alleged he had conflicts of interest, manipulated regulatory oversight, diverted pension funds, and participated in an institutional cover-up involving the central bank.
Peña's deputy, Pedro Alliana, has been sworn in as the new interim president and promised not to "abandon" the millions of people affected by the scandal.
"Compatriots who are now going through a difficult time as a result of the financial collapse will be fully compensated," said Alliana, who will serve as president until 2028.
The demise of the digital bank left more than half of Paraguay's population without access to their savings after it was seized by Paraguay's central bank.
Long lines of people trying to withdraw money from Ueno branches snaked down the streets of the capital Asuncion on Tuesday and Wednesday.
An estimated three million depositors remain unable to access their savings and pensions, prompting public outrage particularly in the capital, Asunción.
Protests erupted across the country in response, with thousands taking to the streets on Thursday to demand their money.
Earlier demonstrations featured clashes with the police, who used tear gas and water cannons on the crowd.
Peña's impeachment passed with 44 out of 45 senators voting in favour of it. One lawmaker was absent.
"It was never my intention to betray the trust you placed in me," Peña said in a video posted on X announcing his resignation, adding his priority was "the peace of mind of Paraguayans who entrusted their savings to our financial system".
Afterwards, senate president Basilio Núñez said Peña was found guilty of "dereliction of duty".
Senator Rafael Filizzola said: "We are facing the biggest corruption scandal in our democratic history – a tremendous blow to the state, to private citizens, and to the country's credibility and image."
Analysts say Peña is likely to now be prosecuted over the bank's collapse.
His defence lawyer Ricardo Preda described the allegations as a "reckless accusation" that was "irresponsible and opportunistic".

articles.title_orig: GE Aerospace Reports US$12.9bn in China Agreements
articles.title_zh: GE Aerospace Reports US$12.9bn in China Agreements
articles.content_orig:
A global review of commercial flight
SHANGHAI — GE Aerospace said November 6 that it had signed sales and service agreements worth more than US$12.9bn at the China International Import Expo, including engines and long-term support for China Eastern Airlines (MU).
Reuters reported the aggregate value and scope of the agreements , citing a GE Aerospace statement. The total covers multiple sales and service arrangements, rather than the price of China Eastern's new-aircraft engines alone.
China Eastern will purchase 202 LEAP-1A engines for 101 Airbus A320neo-family aircraft, Reuters reported. A separate agreement covers 14 spare engines across the LEAP-1A, LEAP-1C and CFM56-7B models. GE Aerospace also reached supply and repair agreements with MTU Maintenance Zhuhai, according to the report.
CFM International's November 6 announcement confirms China Eastern's engine selection for 101 aircraft, together with spare engines and a long-term services agreement. CFM is a 50/50 joint venture between GE Aerospace and Safran Aircraft Engines.
The aircraft will include A320neo, A321neo and A321XLR models, CFM said, without providing an individual delivery schedule in its announcement. It says China Eastern already operates 215 A320neo and A321neo aircraft powered by LEAP-1A engines, making the selection an extension of an established engine fleet.
The airline also uses the LEAP-1B on Boeing 737 MAX aircraft and the LEAP-1C on COMAC C919s, according to CFM. These are distinct engine variants for different aircraft platforms; the spare-engine agreement spans both newer LEAP models and the older CFM56-7B.
MTU's Zhuhai facility description lists LEAP and CFM56 maintenance capabilities . Its separate Jinwan branch, operating since March 2025, focuses on Pratt & Whitney PW1100G-JM engines.
GE's latest financial results show the scale of the servicing opportunity. In its third-quarter results released October 20 , the company reported a commercial-services backlog exceeding US$170bn. Commercial Engines & Services revenue from services grew 17% year over year in the quarter; spare-parts revenue rose more than 20%.
CFM is also preparing for more LEAP maintenance as the installed fleet grows. Its July maintenance-network update described five-year investment commitments exceeding US$1bn by GE Aerospace and €1bn by Safran Aircraft Engines, alongside expansion of licensed maintenance providers and spare-parts inventories.
Those investments address the support needed after engines are delivered. For airlines, access to replacement engines, parts and repair slots can matter alongside the original purchase price. Airways has examined how engine-maintenance bills can remain elevated even as aircraft availability improves .
Neither CFM's announcement nor Reuters' account supplies a breakdown showing how the US$12.9bn total is divided between engine sales, spare engines and future maintenance.

articles.title_orig: The tech billionaires who fled California are facing a new blue Texas
articles.title_zh: The tech billionaires who fled California are facing a new blue Texas
articles.content_orig:
Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now.
Founder Summit begins Nov. 4, 9:00 a.m. ET. Get your pass savings & deals before it starts. REGISTER HERE.
Democrats’ historic victory in this week’s midterm elections could also have a dramatic effect on the tech industry.
In dozens of local ballot measures, voters rejected data centers . And even when they weren’t voting on the issue directly, they were electing politicians — like Texas’ new governor-elect Gina Hinojosa — who campaigned on the promise of restricting data centers.
On the latest episode of TechCrunch’s Equity podcast , Kirsten Korosec, Sean O’Kane, and I discussed what the midterms mean for the tech industry. Sean kicked it off by noting that Elon Musk “seems to have basically nothing out of donating half a billion dollars” to Republicans, while his companies are now headquartered “in a state that has, remarkably, turned about as blue as it could possibly turn.”
And Kirsten said that while data centers probably weren’t the main cause of the “blue wave,” they’ve become an “an increasingly grassroots issue, in part because of how hyperscalers and companies have gone about” getting their projects approved. And now, “we’re already seeing companies like OpenAI all of a sudden go, ‘Actually, we can change our policies.’”
Keep reading for a preview of our conversation , edited for length and clarity.
Sean O’Kane: First off, let’s talk about the fact that one of the biggest data center builders was also the largest donor to the Republican Party. Elon Musk seems to have gotten basically nothing out of donating half a billion dollars — maybe even more, by the time we see the final count — and in fact is now sitting there with all of his businesses in a state that has, remarkably, turned about as blue as it could possibly turn for the first time in a very long time, if ever.
That, I think, is the biggest thing hanging above a lot of this discussion. But, there were also a bunch of ballot measures up around the country that would have paved the way for data centers to get built faster. Almost all of them got shot down, or voted against. [Actually, many of the ballot measures would have imposed restrictions or moratoriums on data centers, and almost all of those measures passed.]
With [Democrats] in power, there is a consensus view, at least in the tech world, that this is going to mean we have a lot of roadblocks ahead for data centers, especially in places like Texas, where [you have] folks like the governor-elect [Gina] Hinojosa, who has spoken pretty openly about this being a campaign promise and something that she wants to focus on once she takes power, now that she’s beaten Greg Abbott.
It’s the thing that I think the tech world is maybe a little too focused on. I’m curious what you guys think about that.
Anthony Ha: I don’t necessarily think that they’re too focused on it, but I understand why it would feel a little bit disproportionate — the data center ballot measures, certainly there were a number of them, but it wasn’t something that was on the ballot everywhere.
And in different races, the dynamic might have been a bit different, but there was this undercurrent and sense that it seems to be an issue that reaches across the country, that is bipartisan in a lot of ways, but that the Democrats seem to have been more effective at harnessing that energy. And of course, there’s all kinds of reasons why the Democrats did so well on Tuesday, but it does seem like anti-AI and especially anti-data center sentiment was a big part of it. That seems like a pretty potent political force.
The next two years, [and] potentially beyond that, are going to be more difficult for tech companies in general, and hyperscalers, data center companies in particular. I also imagine that they have to be a little bit worried about: Is this going to continue to be an issue, not just with the people who got elected this year, but potentially in 2028 and beyond?
Kirsten Korosec: Absolutely. I don’t think that the data center issue is what brought everyone to the polls and led to the quote-unquote “blue wave.” However, I will say that data centers have been an increasingly grassroots issue, in part because of how hyperscalers and companies have gone about getting these data centers [approved] — very secretive, oftentimes requiring NDAs of a elected officials or appointed officials, not sharing information about the scale of a project in very environmentally sensitive areas, including in the Southwest, where there’s very much a water scarcity issue.
So I think that a lot of folks — Republicans, independents, and Democrats —  all saw this as wrong. They were motivated by it, but I don’t think it was a singular issue.
Now, here’s the interesting thing. There was a lot of waving of hands about how [AI companies] can’t possibly operate under any other circumstances. And we’re already seeing companies like OpenAI all of a sudden go, “Actually, we can change our policies.” They just released what they call a compute campus policy blueprint . And guess what? They’re not going to require NDAs anymore. They’re going to share their plans and supposedly operate in less secrecy.
I think what this shows is that when you put up either a regulatory certainty in the marketplace, or at least signals of going in that direction, then corporations will respond. If you don’t do that, they will not necessarily do the thing that we hope that they will do.
Anthony: One thing I want to emphasize is that they’re calling it this [their] “compute campus policy.” And part of what that’s doing, beyond laying out these policy changes, is also an attempt to rebrand data centers, because they have become such a toxic phrase. So they’re not data centers anymore, they are compute campuses, and I’m curious, whether either of you think that’ll take.
Sean: I mean, this is ridiculous. Come on. It’s not going to change anything. It’s going to cause them more effort. For a company that likes to say that it’s no longer focused on side quests, OpenAI still loves to go in different directions a lot. And this is just the latest kind of thing where it’s just like: Why are you spending time on this at all? It doesn’t really seem like it’s going to move the needle.
Kirsten: I have a great idea for OpenAI. Because in the spirit of making threatening things seem cute, they should 100% create a compute campuses avatar, [a] cutesy thing, and then just present that instead of a power-, energy-sucking, water-sucking data center.
Anthony: And if these are just lovely compute campuses, they should just build their own offices there or work next door, see how that works out for them.
Something else that I’m wondering about is, to what extent the election is maybe the second part of a one-two punch. [We’ve just seen] a big shift in how Wall Street is reacting to a lot of these hyperscalers and AI companies and this sense that [investors] are not excited about the idea that they should be spending all this money building new data centers, spending all this money on compute. And so there’s a financial incentive not to build all these data centers.
I’m very curious how that’s going to play out. [From a regulatory standpoint,] it’s probably going to be harder to build data centers. Wall Street is probably not going to reward you for building data centers. But at the same time, to get to the scale that they want to get to, they are probably going to need to build data centers somewhere.

Anthony Ha is TechCrunch’s weekend editor. Previously, he worked as a tech reporter at Adweek, a senior editor at VentureBeat, a local government reporter at the Hollister Free Lance, and vice president of content at a VC firm. He lives in New York City.

articles.title_orig: Microsoft Researcher John Langford Exits as AI Frontiers Group Is Declared Finished
articles.title_zh: Microsoft Researcher John Langford Exits as AI Frontiers Group Is Declared Finished
articles.content_orig:
John Langford, a partner researcher manager at Microsoft Research New York, has left Microsoft.
He declared the AI Frontiers group over, according to Digg , which summarised a post on his blog, Machine Learning (Theory). Langford announced the post on social media on Nov. 6.
The group had about 50 people. It was moved out of Microsoft Research and into Microsoft AI in early September.
Langford wrote that he found places for his team members as well as he could before leaving, Digg reported.
His account does not detail the group's formal status or where remaining staff were assigned.
Langford wrote that he and colleagues created AI Frontiers inside Microsoft Research in 2023. They wanted more organized research after the release of ChatGPT.
Much of the group's work centred on making AI agents function reliably.
Projects he named include Autogen, a framework for coordinating agents. Another is Fara, an agent that operates a computer to carry out tasks.
Shunyatax also described some researchers in the group as exploring ways to improve models without simply making them larger.
Langford described the leadership philosophy in Microsoft AI as focused on scaling rather than research, Digg reported. He said the environment focused mainly on getting, making and refining data.
He conceded the business logic. In his assessment, returns to scale are more predictable than returns to research. Still, he called a scaling-only approach misdirected and unenjoyable, Digg reported.
Those are his judgments. They concern the unit his group joined, not company-wide policy.
Shunyatax reported that Langford's position was not that scaling should stop. It said he argued scaling and fundamental research should run side by side.
Langford wrote that he could not get innovations used, or even seriously considered, while in Microsoft AI. A return to Microsoft Research held little appeal.
He doubted research could reach use from there either.
Langford wrote, in a post Digg summarised, that he is not comfortable being at a company where his research has no path to real use.
He added that there will be no internships with the group in the coming year. He wished well to the colleagues he is leaving behind, according to Digg.
His profile on the research platform alphaxiv lists him as a founding member of Microsoft Research New York. It also names him a co-creator of the Vowpal Wabbit machine-learning library.
A 2023 Test of Time Award at The Web Conference recognised his contextual-bandit paper on personalised news recommendation. The paper describes algorithms that learn which article to show a reader.
Shunyatax placed the AI Frontiers news alongside other senior changes at Microsoft.
It cited the planned departure of former LinkedIn chief executive Ryan Roslansky from his later responsibilities over the Office and Teams divisions.
It also cited the move of former AI platform head Eric Boyd to Anthropic.
The link is unproven. Shunyatax said the material does not establish that those changes stemmed from disagreements over research strategy, or that they are linked to Langford's exit.

articles.title_orig: Berkshire Hathaway buys back $9.6 billion of its own stock but its profits declined
articles.title_zh: Berkshire Hathaway buys back $9.6 billion of its own stock but its profits declined
articles.content_orig:
Berkshire Hathaway said Saturday it accelerated its share repurchases during the third quarter, as operating and overall profits took a hit.
The Greg Abel-led conglomerate bought back $9.6 billion worth of Berkshire stock. That's more than double the $4.5 billion repurchased in the second quarter and brings the company's total buybacks for 2026 to about $14.4 billion.
The sharp increase came as Berkshire's operating earnings — those from wholly-owned businesses — fell year over year, as profits from its insurance business pulled back.
Berkshire operating profits totaled $12.705 billion, down 5.8% from $13.485 billion in the year-earlier period. Insurance underwriting tumbled 43% year on year to $1.352 billion, while insurance investment income declined 14% to $2.734 billion. Berkshire's railroad, energy and manufacturing businesses all saw earnings grow year over year.
The company's overall earnings, which include Berkshire's sprawling stock market portfolio, also dropped 28% in the third quarter to $22.112 billion from $30.796 billion a year prior. Investment gains for the company fell nearly 50% to $9.407 billion.
Despite the earnings pullback, Berkshire stock has outperformed recently amid a massive rotation out of technology stocks. Class A shares are up more than 12% over the past month, while the S&P 500 has dropped 5.5% in that time. Year to date, Berkshire has gained 13%, while the broad market index is up just 7.8%.
Berkshire's five largest equity holdings remained the same in the third quarter: Alphabet , American Express , Apple , Bank of America and Coca-Cola .
Berkshire's cash hoard also grew 3% in the third quarter $377.435 billion from $365.514 billion in the second quarter. However, excluding rail and utility cash along with T-bill payables, the conglomerate's cash holdings totaled $352.3 billion, down 1.9% quarter over quarter.
— CNBC's Alex Crippen contributed reporting.

articles.title_orig: More Than 50 Killed in Yemen in One of the Deadliest 24 Hours of the War
articles.title_zh: More Than 50 Killed in Yemen in One of the Deadliest 24 Hours of the War
articles.content_orig:
Media linked to the Houthi movement in Yemen say that at least 25 people, including women and children, have been killed in airstrikes by Saudi Arabia.
There has been no comment from the Saudi-led coalition backing the internationally recognised government in Yemen.
Live video footage on Al Masirah - a television station run by the Houthis - has shown rescuers pulling bodies out of the rubble of several buildings in al-Shariyah, a town to the east of the capital, Sanaa.
The bodies of young children can be seen among those dug out from the ruins.
The television station has also shown a number of injured people being carried on stretchers to hospital.
Saba news agency, which is also run by the Houthis, said the attack was carried out by Saudi Arabia.
The Saudis have led a coalition that has been fighting the Houthis for more than a decade in support of Yemen's internationally recognised government.
The war in Yemen had been dormant for several years but reignited as a result of the Iran war.
A truce began to fall apart when Saudi Arabia struck the airport in Sanaa - which is controlled by the Houthis - to prevent an Iranian plan landing there.
The Tehran-backed Houthis subsequently targeted Abha airport in Saudi Arabia, then began hitting Saudi ships that have been using the Red Sea off the coast of Yemen as an alternative oil export route to the Strait of Hormuz.
Major fighting has since resumed in Yemen between the Houthis and forces fighting for the Saudi-backed government of Yemen.
On Friday, an attack on a market in Taiz province, which has been the focus of much of the recent fighting, is reported to have killed 30 people.
The Houthis accused the Saudis of carrying out the strike, while government forces accused the Houthis of having fired a missile at the site.
The United Nations says more than 1,600 people have been killed and more than 300,000 displaced since fighting resumed.
The Saudis have regularly bombed Houthi positions, while the group has fired multiple missiles at targets inside Saudi Arabia, including airports and oil facilities.
Hours before the strike that hit al-Shariyah, the Saudi-led coalition said it intercepted a missile heading towards Riyadh.
A Houthi leader, Mahdi al-Mashat, has vowed that the group will take revenge for the latest attacks in Yemen.

articles.title_orig: No clear winner after tight New Zealand general election
articles.title_zh: No clear winner after tight New Zealand general election
articles.content_orig:
There was no clear winner following New Zealand's election on Saturday, as the leaders of its two major parties preparing for negotiations to form a coalition government.
Prime Minister Christopher Luxon's centre-right National Party won 42 seats but was 19 short of the simple majority needed to form a government, despite being the largest party, preliminary results show.
Combined with their coalition partners ACT and New Zealand First, they would have a slim lead over the left-leaning bloc if a deal could be reached.
But opposition leader Chris Hipkins, whose Labour Party won 36 seats, showed no signs of conceding, saying the "shape of the next government" will remain uncertain "for a while".
The tight result followed a campaign shaped by the cost of living and unemployment.
Projections show the National Party on 42 seats and Labour on 36. The Greens are on 16, with ACT on 13, New Zealand First on 12, the Opportunity Party on 7 and Te Pāti Māori, which represents Māori interests, on 5.
The electoral commission was not due to announced the official result until 27 November.
Luxon congratulated Hipkins on a "very hard-fought race" before addressing party colleagues, saying "whatever the final count, we are incredibly proud of each and everyone for you".
He said he would run a caretaker government until the final results were confirmed later in the month, adding: "With those final results there can then be meaningful negotiations."
Elsewhere, Labour leader Kipkins said "the people have spoken", adding: "It may take a bit longer to work out what they've said."
Hipkins said the results made clear the "next parliament is going to require all of us to compromise, to work together and to find a common ground".
More than 99% of votes have been counted in New Zealand, with National and Labour neck-and-neck in terms of vote share.
But the preliminary results pointed to historically low support for the two major parties, with a combined vote share of around 60%.
They were followed by the Greens, ACT, New Zealand First, centrist party Opportunity and Te Pāti Māori, which represents Māori interests.
The Opportunity Party crossed the 5% threshold to enter parliament for the first time, with leader Qiulae Wong saying would work with either side.
It has been described as this election's kingmaker as it remains open to working with either major bloc, but its leaders said they would negotiate first with the party that secures the most seats.
Speaking at Opportunity's watch party, Wong told supporters: "We believe that we can change the way we do politics to focus on the future, on the next generation, and on finding common ground."
Professor Andrew Geddis from the University of Otago, an expert in election law, said "the Opportunity Party as a wildcard player" could "determine which bloc of parties is able to govern".
"It will come down to some very fine vote margins not just between the parties, but in individual electorates. We are going to have to wait for the special votes to be processed and counted over the next three weeks," he said.
Special votes are votes cast outside a voter's electorate, including overseas.
The Greens – who have proposed forcing the country's two main supermarkets to divest stores to create publicly-owned shops – saw their vote rise by a couple of percentage points.
Julian McCrann, head of polling at Roy Morgan, told BBC News the cost of living was the main issue for many New Zealanders
"Three years ago, Luxon came in saying he'd be making New Zealanders' lives better and solving these economic issues, but he hasn't really delivered," he said.
More than half of the country no longer see New Zealand as a land of opportunity, according to an annual social cohesion survey. Record numbers of Kiwis have been leaving the country, with many going to Australia.
New Zealand's mixed-member proportional voting system means most governments are coalitions.
Each voter makes two choices – for the representative of their constituency in parliament and a political party.
